subtype: Approach: assuming silence means loss of interest [Pitfall]
passage: Counsellor's note, written by Ms Fernandes. Joseph came on Monday, tired, phone in his hand. He explained that his girlfriend Meera, in another city, had answered only twice in a week, during her exams. He had started imagining she had gone cold. He sent messages every hour: "Are you angry?", "Did I do something?" The last one at midnight. She replied, "I am studying, please stop," and they argued badly. Joseph said he felt ashamed afterwards. We sat together with a piece of paper and listed other reasons someone goes quiet in exam week. He wrote seven. I did not tell him what to do next. He decided to apologise and to ask, once, how she would like to stay in touch this fortnight.

qa.q: How many other reasons did Joseph write?
What was Joseph feeling when he sent messages every hour?
qa.a: Joseph was anxious and afraid Meera had gone cold, and he felt ashamed afterwards when the argument came.

qa.q: Which choice did Joseph reach by the end of the session, and why might it work better than hourly messages?
qa.a: Joseph chose to apologise and to ask Meera once how she would like to stay in touch this fortnight; it gives her room to study and lets her set the pace instead of answering pressure.

qa.q: How might Meera have felt when the messages kept coming?
qa.a: Meera likely felt pressured and frustrated while studying, since she asked him to stop and an argument followed.

grounding: Shows a student reading a partner's slower replies during exams as lost interest, sending many anxious messages, and starting an argument.

passage:
Thursday, 1:15 a.m.
Nidhi has semester exams, I know that. But she answered my morning message six hours later with just 'ok'. By evening I had sent eleven more. 'Are you upset?' 'Did I do something?' 'You were online at 4, so you're not that busy.' 'Just tell me if you're losing interest.'
At 10 she called. She was crying, not because of me, she said, but because she'd bombed her chemistry paper and my messages made her feel she had to manage me as well. Then she said, 'I can't do this tonight,' and hung up.
Anirban heard the whole thing from his bed and said, 'Jatin, bro, you wrote a novel to someone in exam week.'
I scrolled back. Eleven messages. She hadn't answered them because she'd been in an exam hall and then asleep. I built a whole story out of silence.

qa.q: How many more messages had Jatin sent by evening?
What was Jatin feeling while sending those messages?
qa.a: He felt anxious and insecure, reading her short reply and silence as a sign she was losing interest.

qa.q: What could Jatin do differently next time Nidhi's replies slow down in exams?
qa.a: Send one kind message wishing her luck and wait, reminding himself that exam weeks are busy, instead of asking for reassurance.

qa.q: How did the messages feel to Nidhi?
qa.a: She felt pressured, as if she had to manage Jatin's worries on top of a bad chemistry paper.

grounding: Shows a student reading a partner's slow exam-week replies as lost interest, sending many anxious messages, and setting off an argument.
